meta.blurb: A storm sweeps a Kansas girl and her little dog into a strange, bright land. To get home, Dorothy must follow a yellow road to the Emerald City, with three odd friends who each long for something they already have.
meta.bible: Dorothy: a kind, brave little girl from a Kansas farm. Toto: her small black dog. Aunt Em: Dorothy's aunt, gray and tired. Uncle Henry: Dorothy's uncle, a quiet farmer. Kansas: the flat, gray prairie where Dorothy lives. Cyclone: the storm that lifts the house. Oz: the Land of Oz, a magic country with four parts. Munchkins: the small blue people of the East. Winkies: the yellow people of the West. Quadlings: the red people of the South. Wicked Witch of the East: crushed by the house. Wicked Witch of the West: has one eye like a telescope, fears water. Good Witch of the North: a kind old woman who guides Dorothy. Glinda: the Good Witch of the South, young and beautiful. Silver Shoes: magic shoes from the Witch of the East. Yellow Brick Road: the road to the Emerald City. Emerald City: the green city where the Wizard lives. Scarecrow: made of straw, wants brains, is really wise. Tin Woodman: made of tin, wants a heart, is really kind. Cowardly Lion: wants courage, is really brave. Wizard: the Great Oz, really a kind old man from Omaha and a humbug. Omaha: the Wizard's home city in America. Boq: a Munchkin who feeds Dorothy. Kalidahs: fierce beasts with the heads of tigers and the bodies of bears. Poppies: red flowers whose smell makes you sleep. Field Mice: small helpers led by their Queen. Stork: the bird who saves Scarecrow. Winged Monkeys: flying servants of the Golden Cap, led by their King. Golden Cap: a magic cap that gives three wishes. Fighting Trees: trees that grab travelers. China Country: a land of living china people. Hammer-Heads: rude people with heads like hammers. Balloon: the Wizard's way of leaving. Voice and tone: warm, simple, bright and a little funny; danger is real but never gory; the ending is gentle and joyful.

beats.scene: Dorothy and Toto stand before a small gray house on a flat gray prairie
beats.summary: Dorothy lives on a gray Kansas farm with Aunt Em, Uncle Henry and her dog Toto.

beats.scene: Aunt Em shouts and points while Dorothy snatches up Toto near a trapdoor
beats.summary: A cyclone is coming, and Aunt Em tells Dorothy to run to the cellar.

beats.scene: The little house spins high in the air inside the storm
beats.summary: The cyclone lifts the house, with Dorothy and Toto inside, high into the sky.

beats.scene: The house rests in a green meadow beside two feet in silver shoes
beats.summary: The house lands in a beautiful country and crushes the Wicked Witch of the East.

beats.scene: Small blue Munchkins and a tiny old woman greet Dorothy at the door
beats.summary: The Munchkins and the Good Witch of the North thank Dorothy for freeing them.

beats.scene: The old woman kisses Dorothy's forehead beside a road of yellow bricks
beats.summary: The Witch of the North gives her a kiss and the silver shoes, and sends her to the Wizard.

beats.scene: Dorothy and Toto eat a big feast at a Munchkin's blue house
beats.summary: Dorothy sets off on the yellow road and stays the night with Boq the Munchkin.

beats.scene: A scarecrow on a pole in a cornfield winks at Dorothy
beats.summary: Dorothy meets the Scarecrow in a field and lifts him down from his pole.

beats.scene: Dorothy and the Scarecrow walk the yellow road while Toto runs ahead
beats.summary: The Scarecrow wants brains from the Wizard and joins Dorothy on her journey.

beats.scene: A tin man stands frozen, axe raised, in a dark forest
beats.summary: In the forest they find the Tin Woodman, rusted still, and oil his joints.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman sits on a log and tells his sad story
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman tells how a spell turned him into tin and took away his heart.

beats.scene: Three friends and a dog walk together along the yellow road
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman joins them to ask the Wizard for a heart.

beats.scene: A huge lion leaps out of the dark forest roaring
beats.summary: A great Lion springs from the forest and attacks Toto.

beats.scene: Dorothy slaps the lion on the nose while he rubs it and weeps
beats.summary: Dorothy slaps the Lion, who admits he is a coward and joins them for courage.

beats.scene: The Lion leaps across a wide ditch with the Scarecrow on his back
beats.summary: The friends cross a wide ditch, and the Lion carries them over one by one.

beats.scene: A fallen tree makes a bridge while two beasts fall into the gap
beats.summary: Two fierce Kalidahs chase them, and the Tin Woodman cuts down the bridge tree.

beats.scene: The Scarecrow clings to a pole in the middle of a river
beats.summary: On a raft, the Scarecrow is left stuck on a pole in the middle of the river.

beats.scene: A stork carries the Scarecrow back to the green riverbank
beats.summary: A kind stork rescues the Scarecrow and sets him on the bank.

beats.scene: Dorothy and the Lion sleep among bright red poppies
beats.summary: In a field of poppies, Dorothy and the Lion fall into a deep sleep.

beats.scene: Hundreds of mice pull the sleeping Lion on a little wooden truck
beats.summary: The Queen of the Field Mice and her subjects pull the sleeping Lion out of the field.

beats.scene: Four friends stand at a tall green gate while a guard holds out spectacles
beats.summary: At the Emerald City gate, the Guardian gives each of them green spectacles.

beats.scene: Green streets and green shops shine under a bright green sky
beats.summary: They walk through the shining green city to the palace of the Wizard.

beats.scene: Dorothy stands before a giant head on a throne in a green hall
beats.summary: Dorothy meets the Wizard of Oz as a great floating head.

beats.scene: A lovely lady, a beast and a ball of fire fill the throne room
beats.summary: The Scarecrow, Woodman and Lion each see the Wizard in a different form.

beats.scene: The Wizard's great voice booms while the four friends listen, shocked
beats.summary: The Wizard will help them only if they kill the Wicked Witch of the West.

beats.scene: The Witch looks through her telescope eye as wolves run through the forest
beats.summary: The Witch sees them coming and sends forty wolves; the Tin Woodman kills them.

beats.scene: Crows and black bees swarm toward the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman
beats.summary: The Scarecrow defeats her crows, and the Tin Woodman protects Dorothy from her bees.

beats.scene: The Witch holds a golden cap in her yellow castle
beats.summary: Her Winkie soldiers fail, so she turns to the Golden Cap and calls the Winged Monkeys.

beats.scene: Winged Monkeys fly off with Dorothy while straw and tin lie scattered
beats.summary: The Monkeys wreck the Scarecrow and the Woodman and carry Dorothy and Toto to the castle.

beats.scene: Dorothy scrubs the kitchen floor while the Witch watches from the door
beats.summary: The Witch makes Dorothy a servant, but she cannot hurt her because of the kiss.

beats.scene: The Witch trips Dorothy with an iron bar and grabs one silver shoe
beats.summary: By a trick, the Witch steals one of the silver shoes.

beats.scene: Dorothy throws a bucket of water over the angry Witch
beats.summary: Dorothy throws water over the Witch in anger, and the Witch melts away.

beats.scene: Yellow Winkies cheer as the Lion walks out of his locked room
beats.summary: Dorothy frees the Lion, and the grateful Winkies celebrate.

beats.scene: Winkie tinsmiths hammer the dented Tin Woodman while others stuff straw
beats.summary: The Winkies find the Scarecrow and Tin Woodman and mend them.

beats.scene: Dorothy holds the golden cap while the Monkey King bows
beats.summary: Dorothy takes the Golden Cap and calls the Monkeys to fly them to the Emerald City.

beats.scene: Toto pulls a screen aside to show a little old man at a microphone
beats.summary: The Wizard will not see them, until Toto knocks over a screen in the throne room.

beats.scene: A small bald man in a green hall speaks to five surprised visitors
beats.summary: The Wizard says he is only a humbug from Omaha with no magic.

beats.scene: The Wizard hands out bran, a silk heart and a green drink
beats.summary: He gives the Scarecrow brains, the Woodman a heart and the Lion courage.

beats.scene: The Wizard and Dorothy sew silk into a big green balloon
beats.summary: The Wizard offers to take Dorothy home by balloon, and they build it together.

beats.scene: The balloon rises over the cheering crowd as Dorothy runs after it
beats.summary: The balloon rises too soon, and the Wizard floats away without Dorothy.

beats.scene: Dorothy and her friends set off down a long road toward the south
beats.summary: Dorothy weeps, but the Scarecrow suggests Glinda, so they set off to the south.

beats.scene: Tall trees bend down and grab at the Tin Woodman's friends
beats.summary: The Fighting Trees seize the travelers, but the Tin Woodman chops them back.

beats.scene: The Lion looks at tiny painted people in a white china town
beats.summary: They climb a wall into the China Country and are careful not to break anyone.

beats.scene: The Lion stands over a giant spider while animals cheer
beats.summary: The Lion kills a giant spider in the forest and becomes King of the Beasts.

beats.scene: Winged Monkeys lift Dorothy and her friends over rough hills
beats.summary: The Hammer-Heads block their way, so Dorothy calls the Monkeys to carry them over.

beats.scene: Glinda sits on a ruby throne in a bright red castle
beats.summary: They reach the castle of Glinda, who listens kindly to Dorothy's story.

beats.scene: Glinda points to the silver shoes on Dorothy's feet
beats.summary: Glinda says the silver shoes could have taken Dorothy home all along.

beats.scene: The Golden Cap sails off to three places in a bright sky
beats.summary: Glinda uses the last wish of the cap to send the friends to the lands they will rule.

beats.scene: Dorothy hugs the Scarecrow, the Woodman and the Lion in a sunny hall
beats.summary: Dorothy says goodbye to her friends and clicks her heels three times.

beats.scene: Dorothy runs across the Kansas grass toward Aunt Em
beats.summary: Dorothy lands safely in Kansas and runs to Aunt Em, glad to be home.

A1A2: Dorothy lived on a gray farm in Kansas with her aunt, her uncle and Toto.
A big storm was coming, so Aunt Em told Dorothy to run to the cellar.
The wind picked up the little house and carried it high into the sky.
The house fell in a beautiful land and killed a wicked witch.
Small blue people came to thank Dorothy, and a kind old witch came too.
The old witch kissed Dorothy and gave her silver shoes and some good advice.
Dorothy followed the yellow road and stopped for the night at a blue house.
In a field, Dorothy saw a Scarecrow on a pole and helped him down.
The Scarecrow had no brain, so he went with Dorothy to ask the Wizard.
In the forest, they found a Tin Woodman who could not move at all.
He told them that a bad witch had taken his heart away.
The Tin Woodman wanted a heart, so he walked with them too.
Suddenly, a big lion jumped out of the trees and roared at them.
Dorothy hit the Lion on the nose, and he cried because he was afraid.
They came to a wide ditch, and the Lion jumped over it with them.
Two fierce beasts chased them, but the Tin Woodman cut down a tree.
They made a raft, but the Scarecrow stayed on a pole in the river.
A kind stork flew down and brought the Scarecrow back to the land.
Dorothy and the Lion smelled red flowers and fell into a deep sleep.
Many small mice came and pulled the sleeping Lion out of the flowers.
At last they reached the Emerald City and put on green glasses.
Everything in the city was green, and they walked to the Wizard's house.
Dorothy saw a giant head, and it said, “I am Oz, the Great and Terrible.”
The others saw different shapes, and each one was strange and a little scary.
Oz said they must kill the Wicked Witch of the West first.
The Witch saw them coming and sent many wolves, but the Woodman killed them.
She sent crows and bees, but the Scarecrow and the Woodman stopped them.
Then the Witch used her magic cap and called the Flying Monkeys.
The Monkeys broke the Scarecrow and the Woodman and took Dorothy to the castle.
The Witch made Dorothy work hard, but she was afraid to hurt her.
One day, the Witch tricked Dorothy and took one of her silver shoes.
Dorothy was angry and threw water on the Witch, and the Witch melted.
Dorothy let the Lion out, and all the people in the land were happy.
The people found the Scarecrow and the Woodman and made them like new.
Dorothy took the magic cap and asked the Monkeys to fly them back.
The Wizard would not see them, but Toto found him behind a screen.
He was only a small old man from Omaha, and he had no magic.
Still, he gave the Scarecrow brains, the Woodman a heart and the Lion courage.
The Wizard planned to take Dorothy home in a big balloon.
But the balloon flew away too early, and Dorothy was left behind.
Dorothy cried, but the Scarecrow said, “Let's go and ask Glinda.”
On the way, tall trees tried to catch them, but the Woodman cut them down.
Next they climbed a wall and walked carefully through a town of china people.
The Lion killed a huge spider, and the animals of the forest made him king.
Rude people blocked the road, so Dorothy asked the Monkeys to carry them over.
At last they came to Glinda's castle, and she was kind to them.
Glinda said, “Your silver shoes can take you home in three steps.”
Glinda sent the Scarecrow, the Woodman and the Lion to their new homes.
Dorothy kissed her friends, held Toto tight and clicked her heels three times.
Dorothy was back in Kansas, and she ran to Aunt Em with a happy heart.
B1B2: Dorothy lives on a flat, gray farm in Kansas with her Uncle Henry and Aunt Em. Everything around her is the same dull color, and only her little dog Toto makes her laugh.
One afternoon, Uncle Henry sees the long grass bend as a great storm comes across the prairie. Aunt Em shouts at Dorothy to run to the cellar, but Toto hides under the bed.
Dorothy catches Toto, but she is too late to reach the cellar before the wind arrives. The cyclone lifts the whole house into the air and carries it away like a feather.
After a long, gentle flight, the house comes down with a soft bump in a beautiful green country. When Dorothy opens the door, she sees that it has landed on a wicked witch.
Soon, a crowd of small blue people called Munchkins arrives, along with a tiny old woman. She is the Good Witch of the North, and she thanks Dorothy for freeing them from the Witch of the East.

The old woman gives Dorothy the dead witch's silver shoes and kisses her on the forehead for protection. She tells her to follow the yellow brick road to the Emerald City, where the great Wizard of Oz might help her to go home.
Dorothy packs some bread, puts on the silver shoes and sets off with Toto along the yellow road. That evening she stays at the house of Boq, a friendly Munchkin who gives them a large supper.
The next morning, Dorothy sees a scarecrow on a pole in a cornfield, and he winks at her. He asks her to lift him down, because he has been stuck there for a long time.
The Scarecrow says that his head is full of straw, so he has no brains and cannot think well. He decides to walk with Dorothy to the Emerald City and ask the Wizard for some.
Deep in a dark forest, the travelers hear a groan and find a man made of tin, standing with an axe in the air. After they oil his joints with a can, the Tin Woodman can move again.

The Tin Woodman explains that he was once a real man who loved a girl, but a wicked witch put a spell on his axe. Bit by bit, the axe cut away his body, and a tinsmith replaced every part except his heart.
He says that without a heart he cannot love anyone, and this makes him very sad. He will go with them, and ask the Wizard to give him a heart.
As they walk deeper into the forest, a terrible roar fills the air, and a huge lion springs onto the road. He knocks the Scarecrow over, and then he jumps at poor little Toto.
Dorothy runs forward and slaps the Lion on the nose, and he draws back, crying like a baby. He admits that he is a coward, and he decides to travel with them to ask the Wizard for courage.
The next day they arrive at a deep ditch, with a rocky floor and steep sides, that blocks the road. The Lion takes a big breath, and he carries each of his friends across, one at a time.
On the far side, two fierce Kalidahs chase them, and the Lion is very frightened. The Tin Woodman quickly cuts through a tree that spans the ditch, and both beasts fall to the bottom.
They build a raft to cross a wide river, but the current is strong. When the Scarecrow pushes with his pole, it sticks in the mud, and the raft carries the others away while he is left stranded.
Luckily, a kind stork passes overhead and hears the Scarecrow calling out for help. She picks him up in her claws and carries him safely to the shore, where his friends are waiting.
The road leads them into a field of bright red poppies, whose sweet smell makes people sleepy. Dorothy and the Lion lie down to rest, and soon they are fast asleep.

The Scarecrow and the Woodman cannot carry the huge Lion, so they ask the Queen of the Field Mice for help. Thousands of mice tie ropes around him and pull him out of the field on a small wooden truck.
At the gate of the Emerald City, a little man called the Guardian asks them to put on special green spectacles. He locks the glasses on, and then he lets them in.
Inside the walls, everything seems green, from the shops to the sky, because of the spectacles. A soldier leads the travelers to the palace and takes them to wait for the Wizard.
Dorothy goes alone into a huge, glittering throne room and sees an enormous head without a body. In a deep voice it says that it is Oz, the Great and Terrible, and it asks what she wants.
The next day, each of her friends sees the Wizard in a different shape. The Scarecrow sees a lovely lady, the Woodman sees a terrible beast, and the Lion sees a ball of fire.
The Wizard tells each of them the same thing: he will help them only if they kill the Wicked Witch of the West. They are shocked, but they want what he offers, so they agree to try.
The Witch has only one eye, but it sees as far as a telescope, and she sees them walking toward her land. She calls forty wolves, but the Tin Woodman kills them all with his axe.

Next the Witch sends a flock of wild crows, and the Scarecrow twists their necks one after another. Then she sends a swarm of black bees, but the Tin Woodman stands over Dorothy, and the bees break their stingers on his tin.
Her soldiers are the yellow Winkies, but the Lion roars and chases them away. At last she remembers the Golden Cap, which can call the Winged Monkeys three times, and she uses it for the last time.

The Monkeys tear the Scarecrow apart and bend the Tin Woodman until he cannot move, and then they shut up the Lion. They carry Dorothy and Toto to the Witch's castle, but they dare not harm her because of the kiss on her forehead.
The Witch makes Dorothy work in the kitchen all day. She wants the silver shoes, but she is afraid, because she knows that they hold great power.
One day, the Witch lays an iron bar across the floor, and Dorothy trips over it. One of her silver shoes falls off, and the Witch snatches it up with a cruel laugh.
Dorothy is so angry that she throws a bucket of water over the Witch. To her surprise, the Witch cries out that she is melting, and she shrinks away to nothing but a brown puddle.
Dorothy cleans the silver shoe and puts it back on, and then she sets the Lion free. The Winkies are overjoyed, because the Witch has been a hard ruler for a very long time.

The grateful Winkies search for the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman and bring them back to the castle. They stuff the Scarecrow with fresh straw, and their best tinsmiths mend the Woodman until he shines.

Before leaving, Dorothy finds the Golden Cap in the Witch's cupboard and puts it on her head. With it, she calls the Winged Monkeys, and their King agrees to carry the friends back to the Emerald City.
In the Emerald City, the Wizard refuses to see them for days, and Dorothy is upset. At last, Toto knocks over a screen in the corner, and a little old man jumps up in surprise.
The little man admits that he is no great Wizard but a humbug. Long ago, he came from Omaha in a balloon and landed in Oz, and the people thought that he was magic.
Even so, he agrees to help, and he fills the Scarecrow's head with bran, pins and needles. He puts a silk heart stuffed with sawdust in the Woodman's chest and gives the Lion a green drink.
The Wizard tells Dorothy that he will take her home in a balloon. Together they sew green silk into a large bag and fill it with hot air.
On the day of the flight, Toto chases a kitten, and Dorothy runs after him. Before she can come back, the ropes snap loose, and the balloon floats away with the Wizard alone.
Dorothy weeps, because she thinks she will never see Kansas again. The Scarecrow reminds her of Glinda, the Good Witch of the South, and the friends decide to look for her.
The way to the south leads through a forest of trees that grab at the travelers with their branches. The Tin Woodman cuts the branches off with his axe, and they all hurry through.
After that, they climb over a high white wall and enter the China Country, where everything is made of china. They walk slowly and carefully, because one false step could break a house or a person.
In the forest beyond, the Lion kills a giant spider that has been frightening all the animals. The grateful creatures make him their king, and he promises to return once Dorothy is safe.

The next hills belong to the Hammer-Heads, rude people with heads like hammers who will not let them pass. Dorothy calls the Winged Monkeys again with the Golden Cap, and they carry everyone over the hills.
At last they reach the red castle of Glinda, the Good Witch of the South, who is young and beautiful. She welcomes them kindly and listens as Dorothy tells her story.
Glinda smiles and tells Dorothy that the silver shoes can carry her anywhere. All she has to do is knock the heels together three times and say where she wants to go.

Before Dorothy leaves, Glinda uses the last wish of the Golden Cap to send the three friends home. The Scarecrow will rule the Emerald City, the Woodman will lead the Winkies, and the Lion will return to the forest.
Dorothy hugs her friends, one after another, and thanks them for everything. Then she picks up Toto, clicks her heels together three times and asks the shoes to take her home.
In a moment, Dorothy is rolling across the grass in Kansas, and her silver shoes have gone for ever. Aunt Em runs out of the farmhouse with open arms, and Dorothy says that she is so glad to be home.
C1C2: Dorothy lived in the middle of the great Kansas prairies, in a small house with her Uncle Henry, who farmed, and her Aunt Em, who had long ago lost every trace of youth. The sun and the wind had turned the grass gray, the house gray and even the faces of the two grown-ups gray, and the only thing that still made the little girl laugh was her small black dog, Toto. He played all day long, and she loved him dearly, because his bright black eyes and his silky hair kept her from turning as gray as everything else.

One afternoon, as Uncle Henry sat at the door watching the sky grow dark, he heard a low wail of wind and saw the long grass bending in waves before the coming storm. He shouted to his wife that a cyclone was on its way and hurried off to look after the animals, while Aunt Em dropped her work and cried to Dorothy to run for the cellar. Toto, frightened out of his wits, had leaped from her arms and hidden under the bed.

Dorothy ran to catch him, but just as she was starting for the trap door in the floor, the whole house shook so hard that she lost her footing and sat down suddenly. Then something strange happened, for the house whirled around twice and rose slowly through the air, as if it were a balloon. Round and round it went, high above the world, and Dorothy, although she was frightened, found herself rocked into sleep.

She was awakened by a shock so sudden and gentle that she was not hurt at all, and when she looked out of the window she saw a lovely country of green lawns, singing birds and sparkling brooks. The house had come to rest in the middle of it, and at one corner, under the heavy wood, two feet in silver shoes were sticking out. By pure accident, it had landed on the Wicked Witch of the East, and the poor woman was quite crushed beneath it.

Presently three Munchkins, small round men in blue, came up to the door, with a very old woman who leaned on a stick and wore a tall hat. This was the Witch of the North, and she explained to Dorothy that, by killing the Witch of the East, the girl had set the Munchkin people free from long years of slavery. Dorothy, who had never dreamed of being a hero, protested that there must be some mistake, for she did not want to kill anyone.

The good old woman handed Dorothy the silver shoes, saying that they held a charm she did not understand, and she kissed the girl gently on the forehead, leaving a round, shining mark that would protect her from harm. Then she told her that the only person who might send her back to Kansas was the Great Oz, who lived in the Emerald City at the end of a road of yellow brick. The road was easy to find, she said, and Dorothy need only follow it and never leave the path.

Dorothy put on the shoes, which fitted her as though they had been made for her, tucked a loaf of bread into a basket, and set out with Toto trotting at her heels. All day they followed the yellow road through pleasant farms of Munchkins, who waved from their blue houses, and when evening came a kindly farmer named Boq invited them in. There the girl ate a generous supper, slept soundly, and awoke ready to resume her journey.

After some hours she came to a cornfield, where a figure stood on a pole, dressed in a blue suit, with a painted face, a battered hat and a stuffed body full of straw. To her astonishment, the scarecrow winked at her, and when she asked politely, he told her that he had hung there far too long, bored and stiff, with only the crows for company. She lifted him down, and he bowed to her gratefully and began to shake the straw back into shape.

The Scarecrow confessed that his sad condition arose from having a head stuffed with straw instead of brains, which made him feel foolish and ashamed, and that he longed to think as other people did. Dorothy, moved by his gentle nature, told him that the Wizard in the Emerald City might grant his wish, and he joyfully offered to go with her. So the odd little party set off together along the golden-brown road, Toto barking merrily ahead.

As the woods grew thicker and darker, they heard a groan close beside them and discovered a man made wholly of tin, standing motionless with his axe raised against a tree. Rain had caught him in the middle of his work and rusted his joints so completely that he had been unable to move for more than a year. A few drops of oil from a can in his cottage, carefully applied by the Scarecrow and Dorothy, soon set him free.

Sitting on a log, the Tin Woodman told them how he had once been an ordinary man in love with a Munchkin girl, whose old guardian begged a witch to stop the wedding. The witch had enchanted his axe, so that it slipped and cut off first his legs and then his arms, and each time a tinsmith had replaced the limb with tin. At last the man was made entirely of metal, and he had no heart to love the girl, which had been the saddest loss of all.

Moved to pity, Dorothy agreed that the Wizard might give him a heart, and the Tin Woodman, having carefully oiled his joints and picked up his axe, asked leave to join her. Thus the company grew to three, with the little dog trotting between them, and they moved on down the yellow road. The Scarecrow looked up at the sun, and the Woodman marveled at the world as though he were seeing it for the first time.

Deep in the forest, a terrible roar echoed among the trees, and a great Lion bounded onto the road, striking the Scarecrow so that he rolled over and over into the ditch. The beast reared up with huge paws and bared fangs at poor little Toto, who barked bravely in his own defense, while the Tin Woodman struck at the Lion with all his strength and was knocked flat for his trouble. For a moment, the danger seemed very real indeed to everyone on the road.

Rushing forward, Dorothy gave the Lion a sharp slap on the nose, and to her amazement he shrank back, rubbing the spot with his paw and whimpering that he had not meant to bite anyone. He confessed, with tears running down his face, that he was a coward who frightened everyone with his roar and yet was himself afraid of everything. When the others suggested that the Wizard might give him courage, he gladly agreed to come along.

The next stage of their journey led them to a deep ditch, whose sides were so steep and rocky that none of them could possibly climb down and up again. The Lion, after measuring the distance with his eye, crouched down and gave a mighty spring that carried him safely across with the Scarecrow on his back. Then he returned and carried the Tin Woodman, then Dorothy and Toto, and at last rested, panting hard from his labors.

Hardly had they started again when they heard a horrible growl, and two enormous beasts with the bodies of bears and the heads of tigers came bounding toward them. Fear made the Lion tremble, but he stood boldly at the edge of the ditch to face the Kalidahs, while the Tin Woodman chopped through a tree that formed a natural bridge. The beasts, who had been running at full speed, tumbled into the gap and were dashed to pieces on the rocks below.

When the travelers reached a wide, swift river, the Woodman at once built a raft of logs, which he bound with strong branches, and the party pushed off from the bank. The Scarecrow, however, tried to steer by thrusting his long pole into the bottom, and the pole stuck fast in the mud, so that the current carried the raft out from under him. He was left clinging helplessly in the middle of the stream, a sorry sight indeed, while his friends drifted off in dismay.

A stork, wading lazily in the shallows, heard the Scarecrow's pitiful cries and was so touched by his plight that she flew to his rescue. Taking him by the arms with her great claws, she lifted him up and carried him through the air to the shore, where his friends were waiting with warm embraces. The Scarecrow thanked her, vowing that he would be wiser in the future, and the whole company went on with fresh heart.

The yellow road now led through a meadow of poppies, whose rich scent had the power to send any living creature into an endless sleep, and Dorothy soon grew drowsy. She lay down among the flowers and fell fast asleep with Toto in her arms, and the Lion, whose heavy flesh made him especially vulnerable, was overcome soon after. The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman, being neither of flesh nor of blood, could resist the poison, and they carried Dorothy and Toto out to safety.

But the Lion was far too heavy for them to lift, and they were in despair until a great yellow wildcat, chased by a field mouse, ran past. The Woodman, in his kindness, spared the little creature's life, and the mouse turned out to be the Queen of the Field Mice, who gratefully called her thousands of subjects. They harnessed themselves to a truck the Woodman made, and hauled the sleeping Lion out of the deadly flowers.

At the gates of the Emerald City, they rang a bell and were met by the Guardian, a small man in green who studied them with doubtful eyes and then led them to a room. There he opened a box full of spectacles, fitted a pair to each traveler's face, and locked them with a golden key at the back. Without them, he explained, the splendor of the city would blind their eyes, and nobody went within the walls without wearing them.

Through the glasses, every street seemed to glitter with green marble, and the houses, the shops and even the faces of the happy people glowed with the same color. The soldier who had been appointed to lead them led the weary visitors through the crowded streets to the palace and asked them to wait until the Great Oz was ready to see them. Toto, who had been shut out of nothing before, trotted close at Dorothy's side, looking rather bewildered.

When at last her turn came, Dorothy was shown alone into a vast and glittering room, and there on a great marble throne she saw an enormous head, with no body to support it. Its eyes turned and looked at her sharply, and a voice that was deep and solemn announced that it was Oz, the Great and Terrible, and demanded to know who she was and why she sought him. Trembling, Dorothy told her story, and the great head listened to every word without any sign of pity.

In turn, over the next few days, each of the others was called before the Wizard and saw a different and very frightening form of him. To the Scarecrow he appeared as a lovely lady with silken wings, to the Woodman as a terrible beast, and to the Lion as a great ball of fire so hot that he could scarcely come near it. Each of them, however, was given exactly the same stern message by the voice, and none of them dared to argue.

Oz declared that he would grant their wishes on one condition, namely that they destroy the Wicked Witch of the West, whose cruelty had kept the Winkie country in terror for many years. Dorothy protested in tears that she had never killed anything on purpose, but the great head answered that it was her only chance of seeing Aunt Em again. Sadly, and with many fears, the little band prepared to set out toward the setting sun.

Meanwhile, the Witch, who had only one eye but a most powerful one, happened to look out over her dominions and spied the strangers walking into her land. In a fury, she blew a silver whistle and summoned forty fierce wolves, whom she commanded to tear the travelers to pieces. But the Tin Woodman, who had been told to expect an attack, met them with his sharp axe and struck off the head of each as it sprang.

Furious at this failure, the Witch sent forty crows to peck out the strangers' eyes, but the Scarecrow, snatching them out of the air, wrung their necks in turn, until all lay dead in a heap. Her next try was a swarm of black bees, which flew out to sting the intruders, but the Scarecrow had thoughtfully made his friends cover Dorothy with his own straw. The bees, dashing at the Tin Woodman, broke their stings against his metal and fell dead.

Then the Witch sent her Winkie slaves, who were bold enough but frightened by the roar of the Lion, and they fled in terror to the castle. Having at last used every ordinary means, the Witch took from her cupboard the Golden Cap, which gave its owner command over the Winged Monkeys, though only three times. Twice she had used it already, and now, in her bitter rage, she resolved to use it for the last time.

Gibbering and chattering, the Winged Monkeys swooped down on the travelers, tore the Scarecrow's clothes to shreds, bent the Tin Woodman into a battered heap, and bound the Lion with ropes. They would have harmed Dorothy as well, but they caught sight of the Good Witch's mark upon her forehead and understood that no power of evil could safely touch her. Instead, they bore her and Toto, as gently as they could, to the Witch's castle and set them down at the door.

The Wicked Witch, seeing the mark, did not dare to strike the girl, and since she had no other choice, she set her to scrub the pots and sweep the floor. At night, while she was away, Dorothy fed the imprisoned Lion in secret and wept for her lost friends, though the Lion, with his usual fear, would not try to escape. The Witch, for her part, cast covetous glances at the silver shoes, for she knew very well the power they held.

One day, the Witch laid a bar of iron across the kitchen floor, made invisible by magic, and Dorothy tripped over it and fell. As she did so, one of her silver shoes came off, and the Witch snatched it up with a shriek of triumph, which showed that she now held a share of its power. Dorothy, enraged beyond fear, demanded that she return it, and when the Witch only laughed, the girl lost her temper entirely.

Seizing a bucket of water from the shelf, Dorothy flung it over the Witch from head to foot, and the old woman screamed in terror that she was melting. Water, she cried, was the one thing that could destroy her, and before Dorothy had time to be sorry, she dwindled away into a shapeless brown pool upon the floor. Dorothy took her shoe from the puddle, wiped it clean and put it back on her foot.

Her first care was to free the Lion, and the two ran out into the courtyard to tell the yellow Winkies that their cruel mistress was no more. The people, who had served her in fear for so many years, broke out into delighted cheers, and they hailed the little girl as their deliverer. Never in her life had Dorothy been so thanked, nor had she ever felt so strangely proud.

The grateful Winkies at once began a search for the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman, whose remains lay scattered on the hillside, and they brought both safely to the castle. Their best tinsmiths hammered the Woodman's dents out of his body and polished him until he shone like new, while the Scarecrow was stuffed with the cleanest straw and dressed in fresh clothes. The Woodman, in deep gratitude, was invited to stay and rule over them, but he refused it all for his quest.

On the day of departure, Dorothy found the Golden Cap in the Witch's cupboard, and, thinking it pretty, she put it on her head without any idea of its power. The Winkies, kindly and sorry to part, gave each traveler a gift to remember them by, and the Lion received a golden collar. With the Cap she called the Winged Monkeys, whose King bowed and agreed to carry the whole party back to the Emerald City.

Back in the green city, however, the Wizard refused to see them for several days, and the friends grew impatient, wondering whether he would ever keep his promise. At last, Toto, who was standing at the edge of the throne room, knocked over a screen in the corner, and there stood a small, bald man with a wrinkled face, looking just as astonished as they were. The great head and its mighty voice had gone, and in its place was nothing but this timid old gentleman.

The little man confessed that he was a humbug, an ordinary person from Omaha who had traveled long ago in a balloon, been blown off course, and landed in the land of Oz. The people, seeing him come down from the sky, had taken him for a great wizard, and he had been too proud to tell them otherwise. He had built the Emerald City, hidden behind glasses and tricks, and had been afraid for years that someone would find him out.

Though they were shocked, the Wizard promised to do what he could, and the next morning he filled the Scarecrow's head with bran, needles and pins, which made him sharp and quick. To the Tin Woodman he gave a neat silk heart, stuffed with sawdust, which he fitted inside his chest, and to the Lion he handed a green liquid that he swore was pure courage. Each of them was quite certain that he felt better, and perhaps that was the real secret of the gifts.

To Dorothy, the Wizard said that the only way to reach Kansas was to cross the great desert, and that the best method would be a balloon, such as the one that had first brought him to Oz. Together they cut and sewed long strips of green silk, glued them together, and filled the bag with hot air for the ascent. The Wizard declared that he would go with her, for he had long since grown tired of living among tricks and wanted to see his own people once more.

When the great day arrived, and the basket stood trembling at its ropes, Dorothy ran back to fetch Toto, who had chased a kitten into the crowd, and the Wizard could not wait. The ropes strained, the balloon rose suddenly, and the old man, calling that he could not stay, rose over the heads of the wondering people and drifted away. Dorothy never saw him again, and she watched until the last spot of green had melted into the sky.

Dorothy wept bitterly, for she had come to believe that her chance of returning to Kansas had floated away with the balloon, and no one could think how to comfort her. It was then that the Scarecrow, who now had brains to use, reminded the others of Glinda, the Good Witch of the South, who surely knew a way. They agreed at once to journey to her castle, and the soldier at the gate gave them directions, warning them of the perils of the road.

The way to Glinda's land led through a thick forest whose trees stood close together and bent their branches down to seize anyone who tried to pass beneath them. Fortunately the Tin Woodman, who had been through such dangers before, cut off the grasping branches with his axe, while the Scarecrow was tossed into the air and landed in the middle of the road. After this small victory, the company went on through the wood with far greater confidence than before, and the trees let them pass.

Beyond the forest, they found a high wall of shining white china, and the Woodman made a ladder from a fallen tree, and the Scarecrow was the first to climb it. On the other side lay a strange country where every house, every tree and every person was made of china, as delicate as a teacup, and the travelers had to walk with great care. A single false step might shatter a milkmaid or a cow, and a little princess, startled by the strangers, ran off, tripped and broke her leg.

In the forest beyond, the animals begged the Lion for help, for a monstrous spider as big as an elephant had been terrorizing them, and none of them dared to face it. The Lion, who found that he was braver than he had ever believed, crept up to the creature in its sleep and killed it with a single stroke of his paw. The grateful animals begged him to rule over them, and he agreed, promising to return once he had seen Dorothy safely home.

Their next obstacle was a range of hills, steep and jagged and inhabited by the Hammer-Heads, strange people whose heads shot out on long necks and who struck at any stranger who tried to cross. Dorothy, remembering that the Golden Cap still had some wishes left, called the Winged Monkeys, and the King flew them all over the dangerous country and set them down on the other side. The Hammer-Heads, left far below on their rocky ground, could only shake their fists and stare in helpless rage as the travelers sailed overhead.

In the Quadling country, they came to a castle of bright red stone, whose gate was guarded by pretty girls in scarlet uniforms, and the travelers were led into a great hall. There, on a throne of rubies, sat Glinda the Good, who was both young and beautiful, and who received them with such kindness that Dorothy felt her troubles lighten. When the girl told her whole story, Glinda listened gravely, nodding with sympathy, and then she smiled.

She told Dorothy that the silver shoes had carried a power all along, and that the girl might have gone home on the very first day if she had only known the secret. All she needed was to knock the heels together three times and command the shoes to take her wherever she wished. Dorothy, who had traveled so far, laughed and cried at once at the thought that the answer had been on her own feet.

Before the girl departed, Glinda asked for the Golden Cap, and with its final wish she commanded the Winged Monkeys to bear each of the three friends to the place where he would rule. The Scarecrow was to be king of the Emerald City, for he was wise enough to govern, the Tin Woodman was to lead the Winkies, who loved him dearly, and the Lion was to return to his forest. Afterward, she promised, the Monkeys would be free of the cap for ever, and nobody would call them to serve again.

Dorothy embraced the Scarecrow, whose wit had saved them so often, and then the Tin Woodman, who wept with joy despite his fear of rusting, and then the Lion, whose great mane was wet with his tears. When she had said her farewells to each of them in turn, she took Toto in her arms, knocked her heels together three times, and cried to the shoes, “Take me home to Aunt Em.” At once the whole world began to spin about her in a rush of wind, and the bright land of Oz was gone.

In an instant she was whirling through the air so swiftly that she could only hear the wind in her ears, and then she was rolling on the soft grass of the Kansas prairie. Before her stood the new farmhouse that Uncle Henry had built since the cyclone, and the silver shoes, which had slipped from her feet in the flight, were lost in the desert for ever. Aunt Em, who had just come out to water the cabbages, looked up, and Dorothy ran to her crying that she was glad, so glad, to be at home again.
